text: John Pemberton was a pharmacist in Georgia. In the Civil War, he was badly wounded by a saber, and like many veterans of his time, he ended up fighting an addiction to morphine.
So he did what pharmacists did in the 1880s. He mixed tonics and sold them as cures. His best seller was a coca wine: wine mixed with an extract of the coca leaf.
Then, in 1886, Atlanta went dry. Overnight, his best seller had a problem.
Pemberton went back to his kettle. He dropped the wine, kept the coca leaf, added kola nut... and a lot of sugar. The result was a syrup.
On May 8th, 1886, he carried a jug of it down the street to Jacobs' Pharmacy. There, it was mixed with carbonated water and sold at the soda fountain. Five cents a glass.
His bookkeeper, Frank Robinson, came up with the name, Coca-Cola, after two of its ingredients. He also wrote it out in the flowing script the brand still uses today.
In the first year, sales averaged about nine drinks a day. By most accounts, Pemberton spent more on advertising than the drink earned.
And he was running out of time. Sick and short on money, he sold off pieces of the business to different partners. In 1888, John Pemberton died. He never saw what his syrup would become.
